stories.title: Cyclone Murasu: All 70 gates of Prakasam Barrage opened; 71,000 cusecs released into Krishna
stories.summary: The inflows come largely from the Keesara, Munneru and Budameru streams after heavy rain in NTR district
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Heavy rain continues in the Krishna basin under the influence of Cyclone Murasu.
The Water Resources Department (WRD) has suspended water supply to canals and opened all 70 gates of the Prakasam Barrage to send the surplus flow downstream.
The Prakasam Barrage was receiving 71,000 cusecs at 8 a.m. on Wednesday (November 4, 2026), and the entire quantity was being released into the Krishna river towards the Bay of Bengal.
The water level stood at 12 feet.
To facilitate the discharge, 30 gates had been raised by two feet and another 40 by one foot.
WRD officials have stopped releases into the Krishna Eastern, Krishna Western and Guntur canals as a precaution against possible flooding.
The inflows are being fed largely by the Keesara, Munneru and Budameru streams, which drain into the Krishna from the local catchment areas.
Surplus releases from the barrage began on Tuesday night after inflows increased.
The decision to regulate the discharge comes amid reports of exceptionally heavy rainfall in NTR district and forecasts of more rain by the India Meteorological Department.
Officials are keeping a close watch on the river’s inflows and the situation in the upstream catchment areas.
Residents in low-lying settlements along the Krishna riverbanks have been asked to exercise caution and comply with instructions from the authorities.

Edlapadu in Palnadu district received the most rain in the State in the 24 hours ending 8.30 a.m. on Wednesday, 269.45 mm, according to the Andhra Pradesh Directorate of Economics and Statistics (APDES).

article_sentences: At least two people were killed in Bapatla district after severe cyclonic storm Murasu battered south coastal Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday, November 3, damaging crops across 52,459 hectares and 312 houses.

Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) Managing Director Prakhar Jain confirmed the deaths and said 12,230 people had been moved to rehabilitation centres across the affected districts.
Guntur, Bapatla and Palnadu were among the worst-affected districts.

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Murasu crossed the south Andhra Pradesh coast near Ongole in Prakasam district between 3.30 am and 5.30 am on Tuesday with winds of 100-110 kmph.
The cyclone has also triggered heavy to extremely heavy rainfall across coastal Andhra Pradesh, uprooting trees and damaging roads.
Preliminary reports estimate the damage caused by the cyclone at around Rs 344 crore and the government is monitoring 814 minor irrigation tanks, of which 776 have been placed on high alert.
Kothapatnam in Prakasam district recorded 16.4 cm of rainfall between 8.30 am on Monday and 5 am on Tuesday.
Naguluppalapadu in Prakasam received 11.4 cm, followed by Chirala in Bapatla at 10 cm.
Pelluru and Throvagunta in Prakasam recorded 9.3 cm and 9.2 cm, respectively.
Authorities are also monitoring the Budameru rivulet in NTR district, which had triggered floods in Vijayawada in 2024.
Heavy inflows were expected into the rivulet and people living in low-lying areas were shifted to rehabilitation centres.
Residents in parts of Bapatla and NTR districts were moved to shelters overnight amid concerns over heavy rainfall and possible landslides.

stories.title: Fiery Trump acolyte Ramaswamy loses Ohio governor election after controversial ad

article_sentences: Ramaswamy, who minted his billions in the pharmaceutical sector, had challenged Trump for the Republican Party nomination in the 2024 election, but withdrew and endorsed him.
New York: Vivek Ramaswamy, the flamboyant Republican billionaire and fiery acolyte of President Donald Trump, lost the race for governor of Ohio.
He was defeated in Tuesday's election by Democrat Amy Acton, whom Ramaswamy targeted with an ad that even some leaders of his party criticised.
Forbes puts his wealth at about $2.2 billion and his campaign spent about $79 million, most of it from his own funds in the campaign, where he flew around in a private jet.
An ardent supporter of Trump's fiery MAGA (Make America Great Again) ideology, he modelled his campaign after his brash style.
Trump praised his intelligence and rewarded him with an appointment as the co-leader with tech billionaire Elon Musk of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency.
But in a clash of strong personalities, Ramaswamy quit by the time Trump assumed the presidency, opting to run for governor of Ohio.
While he was initially on the upswing, his standing against Acton, a doctor who had been state health director, began to erode alongside Trump's popularity.
Acton had suffered sexual abuse by her stepfather as a child, before a court ordered her removed from her mother and handed her over to her father.
The stepfather, who was charged with sexual abuse, fled the state and remained a fugitive from the law till his death.
Ramaswamy found her mother, who did have contact with Acton for decades and made an ad in which she defended her husband -- Acton's stepfather -- and called her a liar.
While President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance backed the ad, it was seen by others as supportive of a paedophile.

stories.headline: What Trump's midterms loss means for India
stories.title: What Trump's midterms loss means for India
stories.summary: Marking the start of a new phase in US politics, Democrats took control of both chambers of the Congress at the 2026 midterm elections. The outcome, announced on November 4, came as a big setback for President Trump and his Republican party.This is the first time since Trump's return to the White House that Democrats took control of Congress. Their win came on the back of voter frustration with high prices, a wobbly economy, the war in Iran and concerns about corruption in the government.Indian industry and economy watchers were keenly looking forward to the outcome to try and find out what direction US policy might now take. In recent months, India's trade/export fortunes have swayed in lockstep with Trump's tantrums, making policymakers jittery over any new development in the US.Also read | Vivek Ramaswamy: Decoding a Republican firebrand's high-decibel fallNow, a weakened Trump admin might give India some breathing room. However, it would not necessarily make the road to stronger ties any easier.The big takeaway for India is that while Trump will remain in office until January 2029, his ability to push his protectionist agenda -- as well as his power to appoint his picks for top posts -- will not be the same. This might mean more intense vetting of Trump's trade and immigration policies, and consequently, a reduction in 'tantrums'.It might also mean more uncertainty over future US decisions and potentially more openings to negotiate with Washington.The Democratic victory will not automatically reverse Trump's tariffs, H-1B curbs or foreign policy decisions. Many of these decisions came by way of presidential decree. However, a Democrat-controlled Congress could use investigations, budgetary powers, hearings and oversight powers to raise the political cost for Trump of controversial decisions.Here's what might change for India now -- in trade, energy, visas, defence and other key areas:Trade: Tariffs may face pushbackTrade could be the most immediate area of interest for India. Trump's aggressive tariffs have majorly disrupted trade ties, with Indian exports facing duties that had once reached 50% before the rate on most Indian goods was brought down to 18%.Talks have remained difficult, with Russian oil and Indian agriculture being the big stumbling blocks.Also read | India weighs new oil manoeuvre as old routes get jammedDemocrats might now now look into tariffs' impact on US businesses. While this doesn't mean tariffs are going away right away, trade ties with India might head towards a more predictable path.The point to note, however, is that Democrats are not necessarily free-trade backers. They have traditionally had concerns over market access. So, what happens near term is an open question.Russian oil: Less pressure on India maybe, but no full clarityIndia could get some breathing room over Russian crude. Trump had threatened tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil under the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, before waiving the same later when he himself okayed US purchase of Russian oil.Russian crude accounted for about 44% of India's oil imports in August. While the Democratic win might mean less pressure on India for now, uncertainty in this matter is set to linger.H-1B visa: Greater scrutiny of curbs likelyIndian professionals and technology companies could get some relief if Democrats use their newfound power to challenge Trump's immigration policies.The administration's proposed $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions has been a cause of major uncertainty for American companies dependent on skilled foreign workers.It may be noted that two federal courts have since blocked its enforcement, and the US Citizenship and Immigration Services has recently begun approving petitions filed without the payment.A Democratic-controlled Congress may now increase scrutiny of the economic fallout of curbing skilled immigration, particularly for US tech cos, likely spelling good news for Indian techies and other high-skilled professionals.However, immigration remains an executive-policy domain in several key respects, and a change in congressional control would not itself reverse Trump admin's curbs.Defence and technology: Not much change likelyThe Democratic victory won't likely change the broader defence partnership much. The two sides signed a 10-year defence framework in October 2025, covering strategic convergence, critical technologies, information sharing and joint production of military hardware.Shared worry about China's rise is a powerful unifier for India and US. The issue of closer defence ties with India has had bipartisan support in US, and that is unlikely to change irrespective of the midterm poll outcome.India to get a strategic boost?For India, a bigger takeaway is how and why it should not base its math on who is in power in America.Trump presidency has caused worry for India and but has also given it opportunities. He has pursued close defence cooperation while simultaneously using tariffs and sanctions as instruments of policy.The Democratic win might lessen the momentum of Trump's agenda, but it would not wholly make other existing long-term issues go away.These issues include differences over trade, market access, immigration or India's relations with Russia.India will need to continue diversifying its economic partnerships while strengthening its domestic manufacturing and defence capabilities.For India, the change in Washington could offer more negotiating opportunities while making policymaking more unpredictable at the same time. opening: Marking the start of a new phase in US politics, Democrats took control of both chambers of the Congress at the 2026 midterm elections.
The outcome, announced on November 4, came as a big setback for President Trump and his Republican party.
body: This is the first time since Trump's return to the White House that Democrats took control of Congress.
Their win came on the back of voter frustration with high prices, a wobbly economy, the war in Iran and concerns about corruption in the government.
Indian industry and economy watchers were keenly looking forward to the outcome to try and find out what direction US policy might now take.
In recent months, India's trade/export fortunes have swayed in lockstep with Trump's tantrums, making policymakers jittery over any new development in the US.
Also read | Vivek Ramaswamy: Decoding a Republican firebrand's high-decibel fall.
Now, a weakened Trump admin might give India some breathing room.
However, it would not necessarily make the road to stronger ties any easier.

The big takeaway for India is that while Trump will remain in office until January 2029, his ability to push his protectionist agenda -- as well as his power to appoint his picks for top posts -- will not be the same.
This might mean more intense vetting of Trump's trade and immigration policies, and consequently, a reduction in 'tantrums'.
It might also mean more uncertainty over future US decisions and potentially more openings to negotiate with Washington.
The Democratic victory will not automatically reverse Trump's tariffs, H-1B curbs or foreign policy decisions.
Many of these decisions came by way of presidential decree.
However, a Democrat-controlled Congress could use investigations, budgetary powers, hearings and oversight powers to raise the political cost for Trump of controversial decisions.
Here's what might change for India now -- in trade, energy, visas, defence and other key areas:Trade: Tariffs may face pushbackTrade could be the most immediate area of interest for India.
Trump's aggressive tariffs have majorly disrupted trade ties, with Indian exports facing duties that had once reached 50% before the rate on most Indian goods was brought down to 18%.
Talks have remained difficult, with Russian oil and Indian agriculture being the big stumbling blocks.
Also read | India weighs new oil manoeuvre as old routes get jammedDemocrats might now look into tariffs' impact on US businesses.
While this doesn't mean tariffs are going away right away, trade ties with India might head towards a more predictable path.
The point to note, however, is that Democrats are not necessarily free-trade backers.
They have traditionally had concerns over market access.
So, what happens near term is an open question.
Russian oil: Less pressure on India maybe, but no full clarityIndia could get some breathing room over Russian crude.

Trump had threatened tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil under the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, before waiving the same later when he himself okayed US purchase of Russian oil.
Russian crude accounted for about 44% of India's oil imports in August.
While the Democratic win might mean less pressure on India for now, uncertainty in this matter is set to linger.
H-1B visa: Greater scrutiny of curbs likelyIndian professionals and technology companies could get some relief if Democrats use their newfound power to challenge Trump's immigration policies.
The administration's proposed $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions has been a cause of major uncertainty for American companies dependent on skilled foreign workers.
It may be noted that two federal courts have since blocked its enforcement, and the US Citizenship and Immigration Services has recently begun approving petitions filed without the payment.

A Democratic-controlled Congress may now increase scrutiny of the economic fallout of curbing skilled immigration, particularly for US tech cos, likely spelling good news for Indian techies and other high-skilled professionals.
However, immigration remains an executive-policy domain in several key respects, and a change in congressional control would not itself reverse Trump admin's curbs.
Defence and technology: Not much change likely.
The Democratic victory won't likely change the broader defence partnership much.
The two sides signed a 10-year defence framework in October 2025, covering strategic convergence, critical technologies, information sharing and joint production of military hardware.
Shared worry about China's rise is a powerful unifier for India and US.
The issue of closer defence ties with India has had bipartisan support in US, and that is unlikely to change irrespective of the midterm poll outcome.
India to get a strategic boost?
For India, a bigger takeaway is how and why it should not base its math on who is in power in America.
Trump presidency has caused worry for India and but has also given it opportunities.
He has pursued close defence cooperation while simultaneously using tariffs and sanctions as instruments of policy.
The Democratic win might lessen the momentum of Trump's agenda, but it would not wholly make other existing long-term issues go away.
These issues include differences over trade, market access, immigration or India's relations with Russia.
India will need to continue diversifying its economic partnerships while strengthening its domestic manufacturing and defence capabilities.
For India, the change in Washington could offer more negotiating opportunities while making policymaking more unpredictable at the same time.
That would be its biggest takeaway from these elections.

stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 3: The statements of PDP President Mehbooba Mufti targeting Sher-e-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah are an attempt to selectively interpret history while conveniently overlooking the political decisions and legacy of her own party and its founder, Mufti Mohammad Sayeed. Mehbooba Mufti must first acquaint herself with the established historical and constitutional record of Jammu and Kashmir. As per a statement issued on Tuesday, MP Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan said the Instrument of Accession was signed by Maharaja Hari Singh on 26 October 1947 and accepted by the Government of India on 27 October 1947. The legal authority to accede rested with the Maharaja, who exercised that authority as the ruler of the State. Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah neither signed nor executed the Instrument of Accession. The formal act of accession was the Maharaja's constitutional decision, and no attempt to rewrite this documentary fact can change history. On 8 August 1953, Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah was dismissed as Prime Minister by the Sadar-i-Riyasat, Dr Karan Singh, and arrested on 9 August 1953. His removal was because of growing political differences with Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, particularly over the constitutional relationship between Jammu and Kashmir and the Union of India and the extent of greater autonomy under Article 370. Sheikh Abdullah had advocated greater autonomy for the State, he advocated for separate Flag, Separate Constitution and complete authority of People of J&K except three subjects i.e, Defence, Foreign Affairs and Communication. Sheikh Abdullah strongly defended Jammu and Kashmir's internal greater autonomy He was dismissed and arrested on 9 August 1953 Subsequently, he was implicated in what became known as the Kashmir Conspiracy Case. On 6 February 1954, the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly, functioning under Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad's government, formally ratified the accession of the State to India as final and irrevocable. The arrest of Sheikh Abdullah also resulted in the formation of the Plebiscite Front in 1955 under the leadership of Mirza Mohammad Afzal Beg, which advocated a plebiscite on the political future of Jammu and Kashmir. What followed was a series of far-reaching constitutional and administrative developments that substantially altered the relationship between Jammu and Kashmir and the Union of India. In 1954 through the Presidential Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954, several provisions of the Indian Constitution were extended to the State, including the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India. In 1958 – Article 312, relating to the creation of All India Services, was extended to Jammu and Kashmir. IAS and IPS cadres were constituted for the State in 1958. The jurisdiction of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India was also extended to the State in 1958 bringing its financial accounts and expenditure within the national audit framework. In 1959 The Election Commission of India was empowered to supervise, direct and control elections to both Houses of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislature. The Supreme Court's special leave appellate jurisdiction over judgments of the Jammu and Kashmir High Court was also extended. In 1964 Articles 356 and 357 of the Indian Constitution were extended to Jammu and Kashmir, providing for the application of President's Rule under specified circumstances. In 1965 – One of the most consequential and monumental constitutional changes took place through the Sixth Amendment to the Jammu and Kashmir Constitution. The designation of Prime Minister was replaced with Chief Minister, while Sadar-i-Riyasat was replaced with Governor. The elected constitutional head of the State was replaced by a Governor appointed by the President of India. This fundamentally altered the constitutional position and the nature of the State's autonomy. These were not minor administrative adjustments; they represented a substantial transformation of Jammu and Kashmir's constitutional and political relationship with the Union of India. Prior to entering the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly, Mufti Mohammad Sayeed was an active political activist of the Congress party. He was elected as an MLA from Bijbehara in 1962 and re-elected in 1967 and became the Deputy Minister in the government headed by Ghulam Mohammad Sadiq and in 1972, he became a Cabinet Minister in the government headed by Syed Mir Qasim. Mehbooba Mufti portraying her father, Mufti Mohammad Sayeed, as a mere spectator or a Naive/ innocent figure, but the reality is that he was an active participant in the very political process through which Jammu and Kashmir's Constitution and autonomy underwent destructive and monumental changes. He cannot be absolved of his share of responsibility for these developments. Mehbooba Mufti speaks about political compromises and the erosion of Jammu and Kashmir's special status, but conveniently forgets that it was her own party that entered into an alliance with the BJP in 2015, following the 2014 Assembly elections. National Conference/Congress offered unconditional support to the PDP to facilitate government formation. This offer was publicly reiterated and formally communicated. Yet, instead of accepting the support of a regional party, the PDP chose to enter into an alliance with the BJP, which had a well-known ideological position on Article 370 and Jammu and Kashmir’s special constitutional status. Her father, Mufti Mohammad Sayeed, led that government, and after his demise, Mehbooba Mufti herself continued the same alliance as Chief Minister. What was the purpose of that alliance? Was the PDP unaware of the BJP's ideological position on Article 370? Did it not understand the political consequences of bringing the BJP into the government in Jammu and Kashmir? The PDP must explain why it entered into that arrangement and gave the BJP an opportunity to govern Jammu and Kashmir. The alliance ultimately collapsed in June 2018, but the political developments that followed culminated in the abrogation of Article 370 on 5 August 2019. While the BJP took the decision, the PDP cannot expect the people to forget its own role in the political circumstances that preceded it. Sher-e-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah's contribution to Jammu and Kashmir goes far beyond political disagreements. His historic land reforms, social transformation and efforts to empower ordinary people remain significant milestones in the region's history. His political legacy cannot be reduced to selective quotations or convenient interpretations. The PDP was founded by Mufti Mohammad Sayeed in 1999, during the NDA government led by Atal Bihari Vajpayee, with L.K. Advani as Union Home Minister, claiming to provide an alternative political platform. Yet, when the opportunity came in 2015, it chose to join hands with the very BJP whose political agenda it now criticises. Mehbooba Mufti cannot defend that alliance when convenient and simultaneously lecture others about political compromises. The National Conference has consistently raised the demand for restoration of Jammu and Kashmir's constitutional rights, statehood and political dignity under Article370 and protection of our Land and Jobs. These positions are matters of public record and should be judged on the basis of actions and not selective political narratives. Mehbooba Mufti should stop using name legendary figure Sher-e-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah and instead answer the questions surrounding her own party's decisions and political Blunders which People of J&K are facing today.

stories.headline: Pia Dandiya secures Florida House seat in historic US Congress win
stories.title: Pia Dandiya secures Florida House seat in historic US Congress win
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 4: Pia Dandiya, the daughter of immigrants from Jaipur in Rajasthan, won Florida's 22nd Congressional District, becoming the second Indian American woman elected to the US House of Representatives, after Pramila Jayapal. Dandiya, a Democrat, defeated Republican businessman Casey Askar, according to projections by Decision Desk HQ and CBS News. NBC News showed a 'Projected winner' banner on the race, with Dandiya ahead by about 52 per cent to 48 per cent and about 99 per cent of the expected vote counted. NBC said the race shifted about 14 points towards Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential vote. Born and raised in Palm Beach County, Dandiya grew up in Jupiter, where her parents settled after emigrating from Jaipur in the 1980s. After moving to the US, her father, Dr Rohit Dandiya, continued his medical practice, while her mother, then 40, founded a Montessori school in Jupiter, initially established for Dandiya. Dandiya was raised with strong ties to her Indian heritage, and her parents sent her to India as a child to spend time with her cousins. "Very early on, my parents would send me on a solo trip to India to spend time with my cousins. These trips were life-changing and played a pivotal role in shaping my identity. They helped me understand how different democracies function and gave me a sense of global inequality," she told New India Abroad in an August 2025 interview. After her freshman year at Harvard, she spent a summer teaching English to children aged seven to 17 in the slums of New Delhi with the Asha Cooperative Society. "Teaching those underprivileged kids, I learnt what truly separates people from each other is not their potential, but their circumstances," she said. "I was born and raised in this district by parents who came to this country in pursuit of the American dream, and I've dedicated my career to making sure that dream is within reach for more families," Dandiya said when the Indian American Impact Fund endorsed her in 2025. Dandiya studied government at Harvard and earned a master's in education from Boston University. She taught with Teach For America in Boston and, at 28, became the founding principal of Democracy Prep Endurance High School in Harlem, where about 86 per cent of students were low-income, and every graduate was admitted to college, according to her campaign. "Around 86 per cent of students in my school lived below the poverty. But we promised them a brighter future: if they came to our school, 100 per cent of them would earn admission to college," she told New India Abroad. She was a White House Fellow in 2020, serving on the White House Domestic Policy Council and at the US Department of Education, and later led public-sector initiatives at Apple. Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker appointed her to the state's P-20 Council. This was Dandiya's first run for office. She initially filed to run in the 21st District against Republican Brian Mast, then moved to the open 22nd District after Florida's mid-decade redistricting, and won the Democratic primary on August 18. The district leans Republican by registration, with about 1,85,000 Republicans, 1,46,000 Democrats and 1,50,000 voters with other affiliations, Florida Politics reported. Dandiya campaigned on the cost of living, corruption, healthcare, education and gun safety. "South Floridians are fed up with the rising costs and performative politics coming out of Washington," she told Florida Politics. The race drew heavy money. Through October 14, Dandiya raised about $4.6 million, while Askar raised about $7.4 million, most of it from loans to his own campaign. Askar's self-funding reached about $6.8 million, Federal Election Commission records show. No Going Back PAC, a super PAC funded by MAGA Inc., reported spending about $6.5 million against her by October 24, according to FEC filings. House Majority PAC, the main Democratic super PAC for House races, spent about $7.9 million against Askar. Dandiya won endorsements from the Indian American Impact Fund and Serve America PAC, and from Wellington's Republican mayor, Michael Napoleone. "I've always believed that the person matters more than the party, and Pia has earned my respect and my endorsement," Napoleone said. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigned with her on October 26. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee said on X that she "focused on the issues that matter most to South Florida -- addressing the affordability crisis and making sure that everyone has the opportunity to achieve the American Dream." "Congratulations to @PiaforCongress for winning her election! I am so excited to welcome the third South Asian American woman (along with me and @aishabbwahab) to the House!!!" Indian-American Representative Pramila Jayapal posted on X. Dandiya lives in Palm Beach Gardens with her husband, Navneet Alag, and their son, Sahib. Her win keeps the Indian-American "Samosa Caucus" in the House from shrinking in the new Congress. --IANS

article_sentences: The Court held that the reference has been rendered infructuous.

A seven-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, on Wednesday held that a nearly three-decade-old reference on the legislative competence of states to impose additional sales tax or surcharge calculated on existing sales tax has become academic following the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime.

The Constitution Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice KV Viswanathan, Justice SV Bhatti, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice NV Anjaria, and Justice V Mohana was answering a reference arising from Arjun Flour Mills, which concerned Odisha's levy of additional tax at 10% and 15% depending on dealers' annual turnover.

The core constitutional question was whether such a levy fell within the states' taxation powers under Entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule (as it then stood) or encroached upon Parliament's power to tax income.

Pronouncing the order, CJI Surya Kant said the issue related to the competence of state legislatures to levy a tax on the sale or purchase of goods under the then Entry 54 on the sales tax payable by a dealer rather than directly on his turnover.

The bench examined the entire case law beginning with India Cement, Kodar, the statutory schemes of Odisha and Punjab, and the Punjab Social Security aspect, before turning to the constitutional framework on taxation and the new GST regime that rendered the earlier Acts and statutes redundant.
The Court summarised its conclusions as follows: the reference stemmed from a perceived conflict between Hoechst Pharmaceuticals and India Cement.

India Cement dealt with a cess on royalty in a field covered by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act and did not hold that a levy computed as a percentage of another tax is, for that reason alone, beyond legislative competence.
In principle, such a levy as an increment to an existing tax is to be judged in the same way as that tax.
The premise in India Cement that royalty is a tax has since been overruled by a larger bench in Mineral Area Development Authority.
Consequently, there is no subsisting decision of the Court in conflict with the earlier view.

The Court clarified that an additional tax or surcharge computed as a percentage of the sales tax payable is an enhancement of the rate of sales tax and remains a tax on the sale or purchase of goods within the then Entry 54 of List II.

Subramanyam, 40, was on Tuesday re-elected as US Congressman from Virginia; Miller, 61, retained her position as Maryland’s Lieutenant Governor and Dandiya, 39, won Florida’s 22nd congressional district. Meanwhile, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy was trailing in Ohio’s governor’s race. Americans voted in the most consequential midterm elections, which early surveys predicted as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, signalling a mood for change. Other Indian-American candidates are awaiting their results; vote counting was still underway. Republican Shelley Capito from West Virginia and Democrat Wesley Bell in Missouri's 1st Congressional District have won re-election. Democrats flipped a Senate seat in North Carolina and won races in Georgia and New Hampshire on Tuesday. Former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper won against Republican Michael Whatley. According to some preliminary national results of CNN’s Voter Poll, voters were broadly unhappy with the state of the nation, the condition of the economy and Trump’s job performance. Trump was in his White House office throughout the day with his advisors as Americans lined up to vote at polling booths across the country. On Tuesday afternoon, he shared endorsements for Republican candidates in a series of posts on X. Speaking to staffers and volunteers at a phone bank in Washington, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the Democrats were on the “brink of dramatic change” and on the “brink” of taking back the House. “We’re going to deliver a Congress that actually puts the American people first,” he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was seen entering the West Wing of the White House and indicated that he would not like to speak. In a post on X, Vice President J D Vance sought to remind voters about the Trump administration's effort to cut taxes over the past year and a half. “We ended taxes on overtime.
